body:
What Is a Sustainable City?

A city provides housing, employment, transport, water, sanitation, education and other services to a large population. However, urban development also requires land, energy, water and construction materials. It produces sewage, solid waste, air pollution and other environmental pressures.

A sustainable city meets the needs of its residents while using resources responsibly, reducing environmental damage and protecting the ability of future generations to meet their own needs. It must also be inclusive: essential services should be accessible to people with different incomes, ages and physical abilities.

The concept applies the 3 interconnected dimensions of sustainable development:

  • Environmental sustainability: reducing pollution, conserving water and energy, protecting vegetation and managing waste.
  • Social sustainability: ensuring access to housing, transport, sanitation, public spaces and opportunities without unfair exclusion.
  • Economic sustainability: supporting livelihoods and infrastructure that can remain useful and affordable over time.

The World Commission on Environment and Development, chaired by Gro Harlem Brundtland, presented the influential definition of sustainable development in its 1987 report, Our Common Future. Its central idea is that meeting present needs should not compromise the ability of future generations to meet their needs.

Urban Planning and Land Use

The arrangement of homes, workplaces, markets, schools, roads and public facilities influences how much energy and land a city uses.

Compact and Mixed-Use Development

In a mixed-use area, housing is located near shops, workplaces or essential services. Residents may be able to complete some journeys on foot or by bicycle. When public transport connects these areas, dependence on private motor vehicles can decrease.

By contrast, urban sprawl is the outward spread of development over a large area. When destinations become widely separated, journeys may become longer, transport infrastructure more extensive and dependence on motor vehicles greater.

Compactness alone does not guarantee sustainability. Very dense development without adequate drainage, ventilation, open spaces, sanitation or public transport can also create serious problems. Good planning balances convenient access with healthy living conditions.

Why Urban Green Spaces Matter

Urban green spaces include public parks, tree-covered areas, gardens and vegetated spaces along streets and water bodies. They support environmental quality and provide places for recreation and social interaction.

  • Temperature regulation: trees provide shade, while vegetation can cool surrounding air through evapotranspiration.
  • Rainwater management: suitable vegetated and permeable surfaces can absorb some rainfall and reduce surface runoff.
  • Urban biodiversity: trees, shrubs and connected vegetation can provide habitat for birds, insects and other organisms.
  • Public well-being: accessible parks and shaded walking routes support recreation, exercise and everyday social use.

Green spaces must be appropriately located and maintained. A private landscaped compound is not equivalent to a public park that residents can safely enter. Similarly, planting trees cannot replace proper drainage or eliminate every cause of flooding.

Green cover and green-space access are different concepts. A city may have substantial vegetation but still provide inadequate public parks in low-income neighbourhoods. Accessibility, safety and distribution matter alongside the total area of greenery.

Connection with Sustainable Development Goal 11

Sustainable Development Goal 11 (SDG 11) aims to make cities and human settlements inclusive, safe, resilient and sustainable. Important targets include:

TargetMain concern
11.1Affordable housing and basic services
11.2Safe, affordable and accessible transport
11.3Inclusive and participatory urban planning
11.6Air quality and municipal waste management
11.7Safe, inclusive and accessible green and public spaces

These are targets of the United Nations 2030 Agenda, not a declaration that every city has already achieved them.

Prelims focus

  • SDG 11 concerns sustainable cities and human settlements.
  • Target 11.2 concerns transport; Target 11.3 concerns participatory urban planning.
  • Target 11.6 covers air quality and municipal waste.
  • Target 11.7 concerns accessible green and public spaces.
  • Urban sprawl generally increases the distances between activities.
  • Trap: High population density or extensive tree planting alone does not establish that a city is sustainable.

[Sources: NCERT, India: People and Economy, Class 12 Geography, Chapter 9, Planning and Sustainable Development in Indian Context, printed pp. 108–110; United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs, Sustainable Development Goal 11, Targets 11.1, 11.2, 11.3, 11.6 and 11.7, consulted 2 November 2026.]

title: Sustainable Cities: Meaning, Urban Planning and Green Spaces

body:
Why Transport Is Central to Urban Sustainability

Urban transport enables people to reach employment, schools, hospitals and markets. It also consumes energy, occupies road space and contributes to air pollution, noise and greenhouse gas emissions.

The aim of sustainable urban transport is to provide safe, affordable, accessible and reasonably efficient mobility while reducing environmental harm. Its success depends on how well people can complete necessary journeys, not simply on how many vehicles a road can accommodate.

India's National Urban Transport Policy, 2006 emphasised the movement of people rather than the movement of vehicles. This distinction matters because a road carrying many private cars may move fewer people than an effective high-capacity public transport system using comparable road space.

Principal Sustainable Transport Options

Walking and Cycling

Walking and cycling are forms of non-motorised transport (NMT). They do not produce direct exhaust emissions during use. They are especially suitable for many short trips when streets have continuous footpaths, safe crossings, adequate lighting and protected cycling facilities where needed.

Simply constructing a footpath is insufficient if it is obstructed or unsafe. Accessibility also requires attention to wheelchair users, older persons, children and others who may have difficulty using conventional street infrastructure.

Public Transport

Buses and rail-based systems can carry many passengers collectively. When sufficiently used, they can reduce the number of private vehicles required to move people. However, their effectiveness depends on reliability, route coverage, fares, safety and convenient access to stops.

Transport optionPrincipal advantageImportant condition
Walking and cyclingLow direct pollution during travelSafe and connected routes
City busesShared transport over many routesReliable frequency and coverage
Bus Rapid Transit SystemCan give buses faster, more reliable movementEffective bus priority and station access
Metro railHigh passenger-carrying capacity on suitable corridorsDemand, connectivity and substantial infrastructure investment

A Bus Rapid Transit System (BRTS) uses measures such as dedicated or prioritised bus corridors and organised stations to improve bus services. It remains a bus-based system rather than a type of metro rail.

First-Mile and Last-Mile Connectivity

A bus or metro trip may form only the middle portion of a journey. A passenger must first reach a station and then travel from the destination station to the actual workplace, school or home.

First-mile and last-mile connectivity refers to these connections. Walking routes, feeder buses, cycling facilities and accessible station entrances help make public transport practical.

For example, a metro may be fast, but if its stations are difficult or unsafe to reach, some passengers may continue to depend on private vehicles.

Cleaner Vehicles and Their Limitations

Electric buses do not produce tailpipe exhaust emissions while operating. Their total environmental impact, however, also depends on electricity generation, vehicle manufacture and battery management.

Compressed Natural Gas (CNG) can reduce certain local air pollutants compared with older, poorly controlled diesel vehicles, but it remains a fossil fuel. Neither an electric vehicle nor a CNG vehicle automatically solves congestion, road safety or unequal access.

Cleaner vehicle technology and sustainable transport are not identical. A city can replace its buses with electric buses but still perform poorly if routes are inaccessible, services are infrequent or pedestrians cannot reach stops safely.

Gujarat Example: Ahmedabad Janmarg

Ahmedabad's Janmarg BRTS is an example of bus-based mass transport. It illustrates the use of designated corridors and organised passenger facilities to improve the movement of buses and their passengers.

The central concept is the transport system's ability to serve passengers efficiently. The existence of a BRTS corridor alone does not establish that all neighbourhoods in the city have adequate public transport access.

Prelims focus

  • Walking and cycling are non-motorised transport.
  • BRTS is bus-based, while metro rail is rail-based.
  • First-mile and last-mile connectivity link passengers with the main public transport service.
  • The National Urban Transport Policy was issued in 2006 and emphasised moving people rather than vehicles.
  • Ahmedabad's Janmarg is a BRTS example from Gujarat.
  • Trap: Zero tailpipe emissions do not mean zero environmental impact over a vehicle's entire life cycle.

[Sources: NCERT, Social and Political Life III, Class 8, Chapter 9, Public Facilities, printed pp. 109–115; Ministry of Urban Development, National Urban Transport Policy, 2006, policy objectives; Ahmedabad Janmarg BRTS, official About Us, consulted 2 November 2026; United Nations, SDG Target 11.2, consulted 2 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: A home-to-destination journey needs safe first-mile and last-mile links; poor pedestrian access weakens even an efficient main service.
pictures.caption: An effective public transport journey includes safe access to and from the main service.

title: Sustainable Urban Transport: Public Transit, Walking and Cycling

body:
What Makes a Building Sustainable?

Buildings require materials during construction and energy and water throughout their use. Their environmental impact can also continue after renovation or demolition, when materials must be reused, recovered or disposed of.

A green building is planned, constructed and operated to reduce environmental harm while providing suitable indoor conditions for occupants. Its features may include efficient energy use, water conservation, responsible material selection, waste management, ventilation and thermal comfort.

A building with rooftop solar panels is not necessarily a green building in every respect. It may still waste water, require excessive cooling or use materials inefficiently.

Passive Design: Reducing the Need for Energy

Passive design uses the building's location, form, materials and natural conditions to reduce heating, cooling and lighting requirements before mechanical equipment is used.

  • Shading: roofs, overhangs, trees and suitable window shading reduce unwanted solar heat gain.
  • Insulation: properly designed roofs and walls reduce unwanted heat transfer between indoors and outdoors.
  • Ventilation: suitable natural airflow can improve comfort and reduce mechanical cooling needs when outdoor conditions permit.
  • Daylighting: appropriate windows and openings can reduce daytime dependence on artificial lighting without causing excessive glare or heat gain.

Climate matters. A design useful in a hot, dry location may not perform identically in a warm, humid location. Building orientation, shading and ventilation must therefore suit local conditions.

Efficient Equipment and Renewable Energy

After reducing the need for energy, a building can use efficient lighting, fans, cooling equipment and controls. Efficient equipment provides the required service using less energy than an inefficient alternative under comparable conditions.

Solar photovoltaic panels generate electricity from sunlight. They can supply part of a building's demand, but their presence does not remove the need to conserve electricity.

Water and Construction Materials

Water-efficient fixtures reduce unnecessary consumption. Rainwater harvesting collects rainfall for suitable storage or other uses. Groundwater recharge may be possible where site and water-quality conditions are appropriate.

Some buildings also reuse appropriately treated greywater or wastewater for suitable non-drinking purposes. Greywater generally refers to wastewater from uses such as bathing and washing, excluding toilet waste. Its safe reuse requires suitable treatment and management.

Responsible material use includes avoiding unnecessary construction waste, choosing durable materials and reusing suitable components. A material's environmental impact should not be judged only by its appearance or whether it is described as natural.

Indian Building Energy Codes

The Bureau of Energy Efficiency (BEE), under the Ministry of Power, develops initiatives for more energy-efficient buildings.

The Energy Conservation Building Code (ECBC) 2017 establishes energy-efficiency requirements for applicable large commercial buildings, including provisions concerning the building envelope, lighting and building systems. BEE identifies the relevant commercial-building threshold as a connected load of 100 kW or more or a contract demand of 120 kVA or more.

For residential buildings, the Eco Niwas Samhita (ENS) framework addresses energy-efficient residential design. Residential code development includes the ENS provisions introduced in 2018 and the updated residential sustainability code framework published in 2024.

The existence of a national code does not mean that every building in every state automatically falls under identical mandatory requirements. Applicability and enforcement depend on the relevant legal adoption and building category.

Energy-efficient building versus green building: Energy efficiency concerns energy use. Green building is broader and may also cover water, construction materials, waste, indoor environmental quality and site conditions.

Prelims focus

  • Passive design reduces heating, cooling or lighting demand through building design.
  • Insulation reduces heat transfer; shading reduces unwanted solar heat gain.
  • Solar photovoltaic systems generate electricity rather than directly reducing a building's energy requirement.
  • ECBC 2017 is associated with energy efficiency in applicable commercial buildings.
  • ENS is associated with residential building energy efficiency.
  • Trap: Installing renewable energy equipment does not, by itself, establish that a building is resource-efficient.

[Sources: Bureau of Energy Efficiency, Ministry of Power, Buildings Background, sections on ECBC 2017 and ENS, consulted 2 November 2026; NITI Aayog, Scenarios Towards Viksit Bharat and Net Zero: Sectoral Insights—Buildings, discussion of Eco Niwas Samhita 2024; United Nations, SDG 11, sustainable and resilient buildings, consulted 2 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Passive measures reduce energy needs, efficient equipment reduces energy use, and rooftop solar supplies part of the remaining demand.
pictures.caption: Reducing energy demand and supplying energy are different but complementary measures.

title: Green Buildings: Energy Efficiency, Water Conservation and Design
